youtube.title: What Happened to Saudi Arabia's 170 km Megacity?
youtube.description:
In 2021 Saudi Arabia announced The Line: one building 170 kilometres long, for nine million people. We traced the works on Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite images from 2020 to 2026 and found about 110 kilometres of graded ground, and a pit that kept growing after the work was reported to have stopped. The promise, the Howeitat families who lived there, the costs that rose to 8.8 trillion dollars, and why work is now on hold until after 2030.

Real Copernicus Sentinel-2 images, NASA astronaut photographs and our own measurements.
youtube.pinned_comment: If they restart after 2030, should Saudi Arabia build The Line as planned, a smaller city, or nothing at all?

paragraphs.text: In June 2020, this valley in north-west Saudi Arabia was empty desert. Watch the same ground in August 2026.
A straight line has been cut across it. It runs through mountains and red dunes, from near the Gulf of Aqaba far inland.
This is the start of The Line: one building 170 kilometres long, more than twice the length of the Panama Canal, planned for nine million people.

stat.label: one building, end to end
the length of the Panama Canal (about 80 km)
people planned to live in it

paragraphs.text: We traced the works on the satellite images ourselves, and found about 110 kilometres of them. From orbit, most of it is bare graded ground.

stat.label: of works traced, out of 170 km planned

paragraphs.text: And near the coast there is a pit more than two kilometres long. It kept growing after the work was reported to have stopped.
So is The Line a bold vision, or a vanity project? Here is what was promised, and what is really out there.

shots.on_screen_text: The northern Gulf of Aqaba from the International Space Station, February 2025

ask.text: The Line: a bold vision, or a vanity project?

paragraphs.text: In January 2021, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman announced The Line on state television. It would be the heart of NEOM, a new region on the Gulf of Aqaba.

shots.on_screen_text: The Gulf of Aqaba from the International Space Station, June 2024

paragraphs.text: In July 2022 came the design. Two mirrored walls, 500 metres high and 170 kilometres long, with the city between them in a strip just 200 metres wide.

stat.label: high: two mirrored walls
wide, for 170 km

paragraphs.text: Inside, there would be homes, offices and parks for nine million people, and no cars. A high-speed train underneath would take you from one end to the other in twenty minutes.

stat.label: residents planned
in the whole city, NEOM said
end to end by train, NEOM said

paragraphs.text: Early estimates of the cost ranged from 100 billion dollars to a trillion. The crown prince put the cost of the first phase alone at 1.2 trillion riyals, about 320 billion dollars.

stat.label: early estimates of the cost
for the first phase, the crown prince said in 2022

paragraphs.text: We did the sums. A strip 170 kilometres long and 200 metres wide covers 34 square kilometres. Put nine million people on it, and that is about 265,000 people per square kilometre.

stat.label: the whole footprint of the city
people per km²

paragraphs.text: In our last episode we looked at Dubai, which built a Manhattan's worth of land in the sea. The Line would be about nine times as crowded as Manhattan.

stat.label: of new land off Dubai, our measurement in episode 5

paragraphs.text: And the twenty-minute train would have to average 510 kilometres an hour.

stat.label: average speed for 170 km in 20 minutes

paragraphs.text: NEOM said the design would leave most of the region untouched, with 95 percent of its land kept as nature. But that land was not empty. People lived here.

stat.label: of NEOM's land to be kept as nature, NEOM says
stat.note: An official pledge for the whole region; we found no independent check

shots.photo: File:ISS031-E-30419 - View of Saudi Arabia - Straits of Tiran - Tiran Island - Sanafir Island - Sharm Mujawwa Bay - coast of Tabuk Province - Neom Bay - Neom Peninsula - Neom Coral Reef Island - Jazirat Abu Shushah (cropped).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The coast of Tabuk Province from orbit, May 2012

paragraphs.text: This coast was home to families of the Howeitat tribe, in villages such as al-Khuraybah. In 2020 they were told to leave to make way for NEOM.

shots.on_screen_text: North-west Saudi Arabia from orbit, September 2013

paragraphs.text: One man, Abdul Rahim al-Huwaiti, spoke out against the evictions. In April 2020, he was shot dead by Saudi security forces at his home.

stat.label: Abdul Rahim al-Huwaiti spoke out against the evictions
al-Huwaiti is shot dead at his home in al-Khuraybah

paragraphs.text: Saudi security officials said he had opened fire on them first.

stat.label: said al-Huwaiti opened fire on them first

paragraphs.text: In August 2022, three men from his tribe were sentenced to death for refusing to leave. The sentences were upheld in January 2023, and UN human rights experts said they were alarmed.

stat.label: for Howeitat men who refused to leave, August 2022
the death sentences are upheld
said they were alarmed, May 2023

paragraphs.text: As of the latest reports we could find, we do not know what has happened to them since.

shots.photo: File:ISS031-E-30419 - View of Saudi Arabia - Straits of Tiran - Tiran Island - Sanafir Island - Sharm Mujawwa Bay - coast of Tabuk Province - Neom Bay - Neom Peninsula - Neom Coral Reef Island - Jazirat Abu Shushah (cropped).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The coast of Tabuk Province, May 2012

paragraphs.text: In 2024, the BBC reported that thousands of people had been moved and villages razed. An exiled Saudi colonel, Rabih Alenezi, told the BBC he had been told that lethal force was allowed against people who would not move.

stat.label: of people moved, villages razed, the BBC reported in 2024
an exiled Saudi colonel, spoke to the BBC
was allowed against people who would not move, he said

paragraphs.text: The BBC could not verify his account. The Saudi government and NEOM declined to comment.

stat.label: the BBC could not verify his account
stat.note: The Saudi government and NEOM declined to comment

paragraphs.text: Can a project like this ever justify moving people off their land? Or is that a line no government should cross?

ask.text: Can a project like this ever justify moving people?

paragraphs.text: The earthworks began in October 2021. To see what happened next, we pulled a satellite image of the same spot near the coast for every year since.
July 2021: desert.
By the end of 2022, a straight strip and a new road.
By July 2023, the works covered the whole width of the strip.
Then in 2024, something new appears: a long, dark pit, about 1.4 kilometres long.
By July 2025, it had grown to about 1.6 kilometres. By July 2026, about 2.2 kilometres, and some 60 metres wide.
We measured it by counting dark pixels, so take those numbers as rough. The growth itself is plain to see.

chart.title: Length of the pit, July each year

paragraphs.text: Now zoom out. The works run in a straight line from near the coast, through the mountains, and deep into the red dunes.
Near the coast, the strip crosses the plain with roads, pads and work sites along it.
In the mountains, it keeps the same straight course. It does not bend around the peaks.
Far inland, in the red dunes, there is a second section, graded flat, with large pads beside it.
We traced it all end to end. There are about 93 kilometres in one unbroken strip, then a short gap, then another 19.
That is about 110 kilometres, roughly two-thirds of the planned length.

stat.label: of works, about two-thirds of the 170 km planned

paragraphs.text: That fits what others have seen. In December 2022, satellite analysts at Soar found activity along about half the route.

stat.label: of the route showed activity, December 2022

paragraphs.text: From orbit, most of it looks like graded ground, concrete pads and work camps. Not a city, at least not yet.
We measure places like this from orbit in every episode, so if you want to see the next one, subscribe.
While the pit grew, the plan shrank. In April 2024, the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg reported that only 2.4 kilometres would be finished by 2030.

stat.label: two newspapers report a much smaller first phase
to be finished by 2030

paragraphs.text: Saudi officials denied that the project was being scaled back. In October 2024, AGBI reported a new timetable: five kilometres by 2030, and the full length by 2045.

stat.label: Saudi officials denied the project was being scaled back
AGBI reports a new timetable
by 2030, under a new timetable
for the full length

paragraphs.text: Then came the money. By 2025, the first phase was reported at 370 billion dollars, to be finished by 2035.

shots.on_screen_text: The northern Gulf of Aqaba, December 2024

stat.label: for the first phase, by 2035
stat.source: Wall Street Journal, via Gulf News

paragraphs.text: And an internal report seen by the Wall Street Journal put the whole design at 8.8 trillion dollars, finished in 2080.

stat.label: for the whole design, finished in 2080
stat.source: Wall Street Journal, via Gulf News, July 2025

paragraphs.text: That is about seven times Saudi Arabia's entire economy in 2025.

chart.title: Trillion US dollars
chart.source: World Bank; Wall Street Journal via Gulf News

paragraphs.text: The resident target for 2030 fell from 1.5 million to 300,000, Bloomberg reported. Saudi authorities still said that about 100 kilometres would be built in the end.

stat.label: to be built in the end, Saudi authorities said

paragraphs.text: CNBC reported that the number of workers on active construction had dropped by 35 percent since April 2025.

stat.label: workers on active construction since April 2025

paragraphs.text: NEOM confirmed a strategic review, and called it common practice. The state fund behind it hired consultants.

stat.label: confirmed by NEOM, which called it "common practice"

paragraphs.text: If it were your money, would you have kept building, or stopped and cut the losses?

ask.text: Would you have kept building The Line, or stopped?

paragraphs.text: In autumn 2025, a Swiss newspaper, Blick, reported that construction had been stopped.

stat.label: construction of The Line halted, a Swiss newspaper reported

paragraphs.text: It also reported that the Public Investment Fund had written down about eight billion dollars on its giga-projects.

stat.label: written down on the giga-projects

paragraphs.text: On December 29th, 2025, NEOM cancelled The Line's tunnel contracts. A filing by the South Korean builder Hyundai showed its share alone had been worth 483 million dollars.

stat.label: The Line's tunnel contracts cancelled
filed the cancellation in March 2026
Hyundai E&C's share of the tunnel work

paragraphs.text: In January 2026, the 2029 Asian Winter Games were postponed. They were to be held at NEOM's mountain resort, Trojena.

stat.label: the 2029 Asian Winter Games at Trojena, January 2026

paragraphs.text: Then in May 2026, Semafor reported that further work on The Line would wait until after 2030. The review was led by NEOM's chief executive, Aiman al-Mudaifer.

stat.label: further work on The Line, Semafor reported
led by NEOM's chief executive, Aiman al-Mudaifer

paragraphs.text: The target for 2030 was cut to at most 100,000 residents. About three billion dollars would go to keep building OXAGON, NEOM's port and industrial city.

stat.label: to continue OXAGON, the port and industrial city

paragraphs.text: Officially, The Line has not been cancelled.
And yet, back at the pit, the satellite images show it kept growing into 2026. From orbit, we cannot tell why.
The critics' first point is the shape. A city in a line puts its people far apart.
A 2023 study by the Complexity Science Hub found that the average distance between two residents would be 57 kilometres. In a round city of the same area, it would be 2.9.

chart.title: Average distance between two residents
chart.source: Complexity Science Hub, npj Urban Sustainability, 2023

paragraphs.text: NEOM's answer to the distance was the train, twenty minutes from end to end.

stat.label: end to end by train, NEOM's answer to the distance

paragraphs.text: Researcher Paul Oldfield estimated that building it would release about 1.8 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide. He also warned that the mirrored walls could kill migrating birds.

stat.label: of CO₂ to build it, Paul Oldfield estimated
the mirrored walls could kill migrating birds, Oldfield warned

paragraphs.text: Supporters point to what the design promised: no cars, a small footprint, most of the region left as nature, and a new economy for a country that wants to depend less on oil.

stat.label: in the whole city, NEOM said
for nine million people

shots.on_screen_text: The northern Gulf of Aqaba, February 2025

paragraphs.text: In 2021, The Line was a promise of a city for nine million people. In 2026, it is a line you can see from space.
About 110 kilometres of graded ground, a pit 2.2 kilometres long, and no city yet.
If they restart after 2030, should Saudi Arabia build The Line as planned, build a smaller city, or build nothing at all?

ask.text: Restart after 2030: as planned, smaller, or nothing?
